annotations.description: On turn 1, with Sarkhan (a 2-drop requiring {1}{R}) in hand and Sacred Foundry available, playing a basic Mountain instead of Sacred Foundry is slightly suboptimal. Sacred Foundry on turn 1 (paying 2 life to have it enter untapped) and a basic Mountain on turn 2 would yield the same mana for casting Sarkhan on turn 2. However, playing Sacred Foundry turn 1 preserves more flexibility: if the player draws a white or Plains-matters card, they already have the dual land in play. More importantly, Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon could be played on turn 2 instead of a basic Mountain, giving access to Dragon-colored mana and the Dragon tutor ability later. Playing Mountain first slightly reduces sequencing flexibility, though the practical impact is small since Sarkhan only needs {1}{R}.
annotations.actionTaken: Played a basic Mountain on turn 1.
annotations.betterLine: Play Sacred Foundry (paying 2 life) on turn 1 to maximize flexibility, keeping open the option to play Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon on turn 2 while still curving into Sarkhan.

annotations.description: Casting Burst Lightning for 2 damage to the opponent's face on turn 1 with no board pressure is a waste of a card. Burst Lightning is valuable removal that could deal with an early creature threat or be saved for a kicked 4-damage removal later. With a hand containing Sarkhan and Dragonhawk as the game plan, using burn as face damage this early accomplishes almost nothing — 2 damage to a 20-life opponent without any clock is negligible. This is effectively throwing away a card for minimal impact.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Burst Lightning targeting opponent's face for 2 damage on turn 1
annotations.betterLine: Hold Burst Lightning for removal against an opponent's creature, or save it for a kicked 4-damage spell later in the game. Play Mountain and pass, then develop Sarkhan on turn 2.

annotations.description: Playing a basic Mountain when Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon or Sunbillow Verge would have been more optimal. Maelstrom produces colorless (sufficient for Sarkhan's {1}{R} with existing Mountain) while also providing Dragon-colored mana for Dragonhawk later and preserving its tutor ability. Playing the basic Mountain is the least flexible choice since the other utility lands all enable the same turn-2 Sarkhan cast.
annotations.actionTaken: Played basic Mountain as the turn 2 land drop
annotations.betterLine: Play Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon - it still enables turn 2 Sarkhan ({C} from Maelstrom + {R} from Mountain = {1}{R}), provides colored mana for Dragon spells like Dragonhawk later, and preserves its sacrifice-tutor ability. Alternatively, Sunbillow Verge also works while saving the basic Mountain for later flexibility.

annotations.description: Playing Island instead of Multiversal Passage is slightly suboptimal. Both lands produce the same mana this turn (one blue for Glacial Dragonhunt). However, Multiversal Passage can be any basic land type, making it more flexible for future turns. Playing the basic Island now and saving the Multiversal Passage for later preserves flexibility — but the player's hand is heavily blue with Winternight Stories and Sunderflock, while also containing Burst Lightning (R). Playing Multiversal Passage as a Mountain (or Island) now would be fine, but the real consideration is that Sarkhan is on the opponent's board as a 2/2 and Burst Lightning could kill it. With one Island already in play, playing Multiversal Passage as a Mountain would give access to both U and R, allowing the player to cast Glacial Dragonhunt (UR) AND have the option of Burst Lightning if needed. Playing two Islands locks out the red mana for Burst Lightning this turn. Actually, looking more carefully: Glacial Dragonhunt costs {U}{R}, so with two Islands the player cannot cast it at all! The player's reasoning was wrong — two Islands gives UU, not the UR needed for Glacial Dragonhunt. Playing Multiversal Passage as a Mountain would have given access to U+R, enabling Glacial Dragonhunt this turn and potentially Burst Lightning to kill Sarkhan.
annotations.actionTaken: Played basic Island, leaving two Islands (UU) available, unable to cast Glacial Dragonhunt (UR) or Burst Lightning (R).
annotations.betterLine: Play Multiversal Passage choosing Mountain (paying 2 life to have it enter untapped), giving access to U and R. This enables casting Glacial Dragonhunt or Burst Lightning to remove Sarkhan, Dragon Ascendant before it generates value.

annotations.description: Sarkhan, Dragon Ascendant is a legendary creature, and there is already a Sarkhan, Dragon Ascendant on the battlefield. Casting a second copy will cause the legend rule to apply, forcing the player to sacrifice one of the two copies. This wastes a card and 2 mana for essentially no benefit beyond a second ETB trigger (which creates a Treasure token if beholding a Dragon, but the player has Dragonhawk in hand so they can reveal it). However, the net result is losing a Sarkhan to get a Treasure token - a very poor trade. The player should have played a land instead (Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon, Sacred Foundry, or Sunbillow Verge) to advance toward casting Dragonhawk, Fate's Tempest.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast a second Sarkhan, Dragon Ascendant while one was already on the battlefield, triggering the legend rule.
annotations.betterLine: Play a land (Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon or Sacred Foundry) to build toward casting Dragonhawk on turn 5, and attack with the existing Sarkhan.

Playing Island instead would give 3 mana (UUU) to cast Winternight Stories, providing crucial card selection and filtering. Alternatively, playing Passage choosing Mountain and paying 2 life to enter untapped would enable casting Glacial Dragonhunt (UR) or Winternight Stories (2U) this turn.

annotations.betterLine: Either play Island to have 3 Islands and cast Winternight Stories this turn, or play Multiversal Passage choosing Mountain and pay 2 life to enter untapped, enabling Winternight Stories or Glacial Dragonhunt this turn.

annotations.description: Choosing Mountain for Multiversal Passage means paying 2 life to have it enter untapped as a Mountain, but the player already has 2 Islands and needs both U and R for Glacial Dragonhunt (UR). Choosing Island would give 3 Islands (ensuring U availability) and the player could still cast Glacial Dragonhunt next turn if they draw or play a red source later. However, the real issue is that choosing Mountain here is actually reasonable since they have 2 Islands already and need R sources. The player is at 16 life and paying 2 life for an untapped land is fine. But looking more carefully at their hand: they have Winternight Stories (2U), Glacial Dragonhunt (UR), Burst Lightning (R), and Sunderflock (7UU). With 2 Islands and now a Mountain, they can cast Burst Lightning (R) or Glacial Dragonhunt (UR) next turn. With Island instead, they could cast Winternight Stories (2U) next turn but not any red spells. Mountain seems correct for enabling more cards sooner. Actually, this seems reasonable - Mountain is probably the right choice here to enable both Burst Lightning and Glacial Dragonhunt with 2 Islands + 1 Mountain.

annotations.description: Casting Opt before playing a land is a sequencing error. The player has two Islands in hand and only 3 lands on the battlefield, so they should play a land first to ensure they don't miss a land drop. Opt could potentially find a better land or card, but if the Opt draws into a land, they'll have played the land drop already. More importantly, playing a land first preserves the option to use Opt at end of turn (it's an instant) when they have more information. There's also a Glacial Dragonhunt on the stack from the opponent - the player should consider whether they need to respond to that rather than casting their own spell. However, the main issue is casting an instant-speed spell during their own main phase before making a land drop.

annotations.description: Gem25F Timmy is at 3 life facing a board with Sarkhan (2/2) and Momo, Friendly Flier (both tapped but will untap next turn). Sunderflock costs {7}{U}{U} but gets reduced by X where X is the greatest mana value among Elementals they control. Eddymurk Crab is an Elemental with mana value 7, so Sunderflock costs just {U}{U} - so the cast is actually affordable. However, Sunderflock returns all non-Elemental creatures to owners' hands when it enters. This bounces their own Eddymurk Crab (wait - Eddymurk Crab IS an Elemental, so it stays). It bounces Sarkhan and Momo on the opponent's side. This is actually a strong defensive play at 3 life. But the key issue is sequencing: they should play a land first (Island or Spirebluff Canal) before casting spells. They have 5 untapped lands and Sunderflock costs {U}{U} with the reduction, so they have plenty of mana either way. But playing land first is strictly better for having more mana available for Burst Lightning or other follow-ups. Actually, looking more carefully - they chose Sunderflock before playing a land drop. With Sunderflock costing only UU after the Elemental reduction, they can cast it and still have 3 lands untapped, then play their land for 4 untapped lands total. If they play land first they'd have 4 untapped after casting Sunderflock. The difference matters because they have Burst Lightning (R) in hand and might want to hold up mana. Playing land first before casting the spell is strictly better sequencing. This is a minor sequencing error - casting before land drop.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Sunderflock before playing a land for the turn
annotations.betterLine: Play Island or Spirebluff Canal first (to maximize available mana for potential Burst Lightning or other responses), then cast Sunderflock for {U}{U}

annotations.description: At 3 life, Gem25F Timmy is in a very precarious position. They have Sunderflock (5/5 flying) and Eddymurk Crab (5/5) on board, and the opponent is at 18 life. Sending 2 damage to the opponent's face with Burst Lightning brings them to 16, but this is unlikely to matter much when you need to deal 16 more damage. Meanwhile, the opponent has untapped lands (Sunbillow Verge and a Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon) and could potentially play threats or removal. However, there are no enemy creatures on the battlefield to target with Burst Lightning, so targeting face is the only productive use. The opponent's board has no creatures, so keeping Burst Lightning for defensive purposes (e.g., killing a small creature that attacks) could be more valuable at 3 life. That said, with no creatures to target, going face is reasonable. The main question is whether holding the Burst Lightning for later defensive use would have been better than casting it now, but since it's already on the stack (suggesting it was cast during combat, possibly to use mana), this is a minor efficiency question.

annotations.betterLine: At 3 life, holding Burst Lightning as potential removal for an incoming threat could be more valuable than dealing 2 face damage when the opponent is at 18. The 2 damage is unlikely to matter for the race, but killing a future attacker could save your life.

Tapping your own creature is almost never beneficial; it prevents that Crab from attacking or blocking this turn. At 3 life against Dragonhawk (5/5 flyer), blocking options are critical, and having an untapped 5/5 could be relevant for defense.
